# DECISIONS

Short ADRs for calls the brief left open. Each records: context, decision, trade-off, and how the agent was steered to it.
Status: **Accepted** unless noted. Newest last.

---

## ADR-001 — Tooling versions are pinned, not `latest`
**Context.** On 2026-09-17 `npm view` showed `prisma@latest = 8.0.0-rc.15` (a release candidate) while `@prisma/client@latest = 7.10.0`. `typescript@latest = 7.0.2`, but `ts-jest` peers `<7` and `@nestjs/cli` ships `~6.0.2`.
**Decision.** Pin `prisma` and `@prisma/client` (and `@prisma/adapter-pg`) to exactly `7.10.0`; TypeScript `6.0.x` as generated by Nest CLI 12.
**Trade-off.** Miss newer features; must bump deliberately.
**Steering.** A naive `npm i prisma @prisma/client` would install mismatched CLI/client majors. Caught by checking dist-tags before installing; rule added to `CLAUDE.md`.

## ADR-002 — Vendor agent skills installed by `prisma init` were removed
**Context.** `prisma init` (7.10) silently downloaded 9 skills from `github.com/prisma/skills` into `backend/.agents`, symlinked into `.claude/skills` and `.windsurf/skills`. Several target products we don't use (MongoDB, Prisma Postgres cloud, Compute) and would bias agents toward them.
**Decision.** Not committed. Reviewed the v7 ESM/config/adapter references once, then moved them out of the repo. Our agent context lives only in `CLAUDE.md` and `/.agent/`.
**Trade-off.** Lose vendor guidance an agent might have used; we keep the agent's context deliberate and reviewable.

## ADR-003 — Ports: frontend 3000, backend 4000
**Context.** The Auth0 client's callback/logout URLs are fixed to `http://localhost:3000`, so the SPA must be served on 3000.
**Decision.** Vite dev server on `3000`; API on `4000`; CORS allows only `http://localhost:3000`.

## ADR-004 — Resource IDs are UUID v4
**Context.** The privacy invariant includes "must not learn of the existence of" another user's data.
**Decision.** Native Postgres `uuid` primary keys generated server-side. Sequential ints would leak other users' activity volume (my next id minus my last id). Malformed ids return `404`, not `400`, so id shape reveals nothing either.
**Trade-off.** Larger index keys; not human-friendly in URLs.

## ADR-005 — Deleting a collection deletes its bookmarks (with UI confirmation)
**Context.** §3.3: "A user can delete a collection." Options were cascade, set-null (uncategorise), block-if-non-empty.
**Decision.** `DELETE /collections/:id` **cascades** to the bookmarks inside it and to any shares of it. The frontend shows a confirmation dialog stating how many bookmarks will be deleted before calling the API.
**Trade-off.** One confirmed action destroys data; no undo/soft-delete. The dialog is UX only — the API does not require a confirmation flag, so API clients get no second chance. Chosen for a simple, predictable model: a collection *owns* its bookmarks.
**Consequence for integrity.** Cascade lets us enforce "a bookmark's collection has the same owner" with a composite foreign key `(collectionId, ownerId) → Collection(id, ownerId)`. (A set-null action on that composite FK would also try to null `ownerId`, which is one reason set-null was harder here.)

## ADR-006 — Sharing: read-only share of a collection to another user, by verified email
**Context.** §3.3: "A user may want to share a collection with someone else." This directly tensions with §3's invariant ("everything is private to the person who created it").
**Decision.** Ship a narrow, explicit exception:
- The **owner** can grant **read-only** access to one collection to a person identified by **email**, and revoke it.
- A grantee can list collections shared with them and read those collections' bookmarks. They can never create, update, delete, or re-share.
- Grantee access is served from a **separate route namespace** (`/shared/...`). The owner routes (`/collections`, `/bookmarks`) stay strictly owner-only, so the exception is visible in one place and cannot leak into write paths.
- A share only matches an authenticated user whose email claim is **verified** (`email_verified=true`). Otherwise anyone who can register an account with the victim's address would receive their shares.
- **No user enumeration.** Creating a share returns the same `201` whether or not that email belongs to a registered user; the grant takes effect once that verified user signs in. Owners cannot look up users.
- Sharing with your own email is rejected (`400`). Deleting the collection removes its shares (cascade).
- Grantees see the owner's display email (so they know who shared) but never internal ids of other users, nor the list of other grantees.

**Trade-off.** Adds a second access path — the biggest source of privacy risk in the app — so every shared route needs cross-user tests (non-grantee, revoked grantee, unverified-email grantee, write attempts). Email-based grants to not-yet-registered people are stored as pending, which the owner cannot distinguish from active ones (the price of no enumeration). No share links, no edit permission, no notifications.
**Invariant restated.** Data is private to its owner, *except* collections the owner has explicitly shared read-only with a verified email.
